query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The structural and chemical stability of multi-element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is governed by the high configurational entropy that, together with sluggish diffusion kinetics (stemming from severe lattice distortion), inhibits elemental segregation and phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized as disordered, near‐equiatomic solid solutions with homogeneous elemental mixing.
generation.intervention: Use high‐temperature in situ characterization techniques (e.g., in situ TEM or synchrotron X‐ray diffraction) to monitor real‐time atomic-scale changes in elemental distribution and crystal structure during controlled heating.
generation.conditions: Expose the nanoparticles to temperatures spanning operation regimes (773–1173 K for catalytic applications and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications) under controlled atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale elemental distributions and subtle lattice distortions that signal the onset of segregation or phase change.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered state while kinetic barriers (slow atomic diffusion due to lattice distortions) prevent significant elemental segregation. Hence, under service conditions, nanoparticles with sufficiently robust diffusion barriers exhibit minimal phase evolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline where diffusion is unimpeded, nanoparticles with strong entropy stabilization will show minimal elemental segregation and maintain a disordered solid-solution structure during in situ heating. Conversely, samples lacking such barriers (or under excessively high temperatures) will display measurable phase separation or the emergence of ordered structures.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with similar compositions but processed to promote diffusion (e.g., pre-annealed to relax kinetic barriers) would exhibit progressive elemental segregation and phase transitions under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: This stabilization holds within the specified temperature windows and exposure times; at temperatures significantly beyond these limits or under prolonged thermal stress, diffusion may overcome kinetic barriers, leading to segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact influence of low noble-metal content on diffusion dynamics is not fully quantified and could variably affect the kinetic barriers.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near‐equiatomic nanoparticles: one set as synthesized (with expected high kinetic barriers) and another set subjected to an annealing treatment designed to reduce lattice distortions. Then, perform in situ high‐temperature TEM or synchrotron X‐ray diffraction to monitor elemental segregation and phase evolution over the temperature ranges identified.
measurements: Real-time elemental mapping using in situ TEM or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
Phase identification and lattice parameter measurements via synchrotron X-ray diffraction
Comparative kinetics of phase transition or segregation rates between the two sets
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ measurements reveal that nanoparticles with the expected high kinetic barriers (as-synthesized) undergo significant elemental segregation and phase transitions comparable to the annealed samples, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy and kinetic sluggishness govern the stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system.
